name: Pineal gland
function: Midline epithalamic endocrine organ secreting melatonin with a daily rhythm under multisynaptic SCN/autonomic control. Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion mediate an important neural input. Pineal calcification is variable and can serve as an imaging landmark.

afferent: Circadian autonomic pathway: SCN/hypothalamic networks to spinal sympathetic neurons and superior cervical ganglion; postganglionic sympathetic fibers to the pineal gland
efferent: Melatonin released into circulation and CSF

bloodSupply: Medial posterior choroidal arteries (collicular/quadrigeminal region); venous drainage to the internal cerebral veins and great vein of Galen.

clinical.syndrome: Pineal region tumor with gaze palsy
clinical.findings: Germinomas and pineal parenchymal tumors may compress dorsal midbrain and/or cerebral aqueduct. Dorsal involvement can produce some combination of upgaze paresis, light-near dissociation, lid retraction, and convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud pattern); aqueduct obstruction can cause hydrocephalus. Findings depend on tumor extent.
clinical.note: mass effect, not a primary vascular syndrome

clinical.findings: Pinealectomy or sympathetic interruption (Horner syndrome, cervical cord injury) blunts nocturnal melatonin and disorganizes sleep phase.

A mass near the posterior third ventricle may obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus with headache, nausea/vomiting, papilledema, or other raised-pressure findings. Ocular motor or other focal signs may coexist; no fixed symptom order is established.

name: Pineal body (context silhouette)
function: Renderable silhouette of the midline pineal-epithalamic block that sits between the habenular trigones in the posterior wall of the third ventricle, above the superior colliculi and rostral to the quadrigeminal cistern. It exists so the epithalamic dorsal midline is a named, selectable body in the 3D scene; the endocrine organ and its melatonin physiology belong to nuc-pineal-gland, and the habenular complex to nuc-habenula.

name: Habenular nuclei
function: Paired medial and lateral habenular nuclei at the posterior dorsomedial thalamic border. They receive limbic/basal-forebrain inputs through the stria medullaris and project through the fasciculus retroflexus toward interpeduncular and other midbrain targets. Reward/aversion roles are supported particularly by experimental and translational studies; they are not a single anti-reward center.

afferent: Limbic/basal-forebrain afferents through the stria medullaris thalami
Hypothalamic and basal-ganglia-related inputs
efferent: Fasciculus retroflexus toward the interpeduncular nucleus and midbrain circuits
Lateral habenular outputs influence dopamine/serotonin systems through direct and indirect circuits, rather than being uniformly direct inhibitory projections

bloodSupply: Medial posterior choroidal artery (PCA branches) at the epithalamic dorsal midline.

clinical.findings: Habenular circuits are studied in reward prediction, aversion and psychiatric disease. Depression is not a diagnosis of isolated habenular hyperactivity, and stimulation remains a research context rather than an established atlas lesion syndrome.

name: Stria medullaris thalami
function: Limbic afferent bundle running along the dorsomedial thalamic border from septal, preoptic, basal-forebrain, and hypothalamic regions to the habenular complex. Medial and lateral habenular circuits have distinct inputs and outputs; the entire bundle is not a single anti-reward pathway.

afferent: Septal/basal-forebrain and preoptic/hypothalamic limbic inputs
efferent: Habenular nuclei; their outputs leave in the distinct fasciculus retroflexus

bloodSupply: Medial posterior choroidal branches of the PCA (dorsal thalamic/epithalamic margin).

clinical.findings: This afferent bundle links basal-forebrain/hypothalamic regions with the habenula. A specific isolated human lesion syndrome or routine OCD DBS indication is not established by this anatomy.

name: Posterior commissure
function: Dorsal midline fiber decussation at the entrance to the cerebral aqueduct that crosses pretectal and posterior thalamic fibers coordinating bilateral vertical gaze — most critically linking the riMLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal of the two sides for upgaze and pupillomotor symmetry.

afferent: Pretectal nuclei (pupillomotor interneurons)
riMLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal (vertical gaze fibers)
Posterior thalamic nuclei
efferent: Contralateral riMLF, interstitial nucleus of Cajal and oculomotor complex (bilateral vertical eye-movement coordination)

bloodSupply: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA (P1/P2) and the medial posterior choroidal artery.

clinical.findings: Compression or injury near the posterior commissure/pretectum can impair upward gaze and pupillary light responses, with variable convergence-retraction movements, lid retraction or skew. Convergence is not invariably abolished.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, pupillary circuits, printed pp. 576-580 (PDF pp. 602-606).

name: Subthalamic nucleus
function: Biconvex, lens-shaped excitatory hub of the indirect basal-ganglia pathway: glutamatergic STN neurons drive GPi/SNr output, raising the thalamocortical brake on movement; loss of this drive disinhibits the motor thalamus and releases violent involuntary movement. The hyperdirect cortex-STN loop also gates movement cancellation.

afferent: Lateral segment of the globus pallidus externus (GPe) (indirect pathway)
Motor cortex via the hyperdirect (corticosubthalamic) pathway
Substantia nigra pars compacta (dopaminergic modulation)
efferent: Globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata (excitatory, glutamatergic)
Reciprocal projections back to the globus pallidus externus (GPe)

bloodSupply: Small perforating branches of the posterior communicating artery and the anterior choroidal artery (rostral/lateral STN); P1/PCA perforators caudally.

clinical.findings: Contralateral STN-region injury is a classic cause of flinging/choreic movements, but lesions elsewhere in basal-ganglia networks also cause them. Hyperglycemia-associated cases often involve striatum. Evolution and additional signs vary.

STN stimulation is a clinical target for selected patients with Parkinson disease. Benefits and adverse effects depend on patient selection, stimulated circuitry and treatment settings; this schematic is not a targeting guide.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, basal-ganglia connections and Forel fields, printed pp. 748-755 (PDF pp. 774-781).

name: Zona incerta
function: Thin subthalamic gray-matter sheet dorsal to the subthalamic nucleus and ventral to thalamus, adjacent to thalamic and lenticular fasciculi. It has broad sensory, motor and brainstem connections; its subregional functions are not fully represented by this atlas. H1 lies mainly dorsal and H2 ventral to the zona incerta, rather than both simply traversing it.

afferent: Cerebellar nuclei (fastigial and interposed, via superior cerebellar peduncle collaterals)
Pretectum and spinal/trigeminal sensory inputs
Basal ganglia and motor cortex
efferent: Thalamus (intralaminar and relay nuclei)
Superior colliculus and pretectum
Brainstem autonomic and reticular nuclei

bloodSupply: Posterior communicating and anterior choroidal perforators; thalamogeniculate/paramedian PCA branches caudally.

clinical.findings: The posterior subthalamic area, including caudal ZI and adjacent cerebellothalamic fibers, has been investigated as a tremor-stimulation target. Benefit and adverse effects cannot be attributed to ZI alone or assumed equivalent to another procedure.
Larger regional lesions can combine motor, sensory and coordination findings according to adjacent pathways; these are not specific isolated-ZI syndromes.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, basal-ganglia connections and Forel fields, printed pp. 748-755 (PDF pp. 774-781).

name: Fields of Forel (H1/H2)
function: Subthalamic white-matter fields associated with pallidal and cerebellar output. H2 (lenticular fasciculus) penetrates the internal capsule and runs dorsal to STN/ventral to ZI. Pallidal fibers from H2 and the ansa lenticularis converge in the prerubral field H, then enter the motor thalamus through H1 (thalamic fasciculus), which also includes cerebellothalamic fibers.
contextNote: Schematic context record for the H1/H2 white-matter regions around zona incerta. The source textbook labels the convergence area prerubral field H; numerical variants such as H3 are not used here. This silhouette is not a validated stereotactic target.

afferent: Globus pallidus internus via the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus (H2)
Dentate nucleus via the superior cerebellar peduncle (cerebellothalamic fibers share the field)
efferent: Ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamic nuclei via the thalamic fasciculus (H1)

bloodSupply: Perforating branches of the posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries.

clinical.findings: Damage can interrupt basal-ganglia or cerebellar output toward motor thalamus. Consequences depend on the involved fibers; lesion effects should not be assumed to reproduce pallidotomy or a specific movement disorder.
Forel-field procedures have historical use in movement-disorder surgery. The atlas schematic is not a patient-specific target or treatment plan.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, basal-ganglia connections and Forel fields, printed pp. 748-755 (PDF pp. 774-781).

name: Third ventricle
function: The narrow midline CSF cavity between the paired thalami, extending from the lamina terminalis and optic chiasm to the pineal recess and aqueduct; its choroid plexus secretes CSF, the interventricular foramina of Monro drain both lateral ventricles into it, and its walls carry the midline thalamic nuclei and hypothalamus.

afferent: Lateral ventricles via the interventricular foramina of Monro
efferent: Cerebral aqueduct (to the fourth ventricle)

bloodSupply: The ventricular lumen is a CSF cavity, not perfused tissue. Adjacent hypothalamus receives variable ICA/ACA/posterior communicating contributions; adjacent thalamus receives PCA/posterior communicating contributions. Choroid plexus has its own vascular supply.

clinical.syndrome: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
clinical.findings: A foramen-of-Monro cyst traps the lateral ventricles — episodic headache, papilledema and gait failure; acute blockage can cause sudden deterioration or death.
Obstruction at the caudal third ventricle dilates the third and lateral ventricles (non-communicating hydrocephalus) with normal fourth ventricle.
Bilateral thalamic gliomas or hypothalamic tumors narrow the slit, presenting with hydrocephalus plus endocrine and visual deficits.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 5, ventricular system, printed pp. 132-137 (PDF pp. 158-163).

name: Cerebral aqueduct
function: Narrow CSF channel through the midbrain connecting third and fourth ventricles, surrounded by periaqueductal gray and lacking choroid plexus. Stenosis or compression can cause upstream obstructive hydrocephalus.

afferent: Third ventricle at the plane of the posterior commissure
efferent: Fourth ventricle at the pontomesencephalic isthmus

bloodSupply: The CSF lumen is not perfused tissue. Surrounding midbrain tissue receives variable PCA, SCA and basilar perforator contributions.

clinical.findings: Aqueductal stenosis or external compression can enlarge the upstream third and lateral ventricles. Headache, vomiting or other raised-pressure signs may occur. Gaze palsy or ataxia depends on associated midbrain/cerebellar involvement and is not an obligatory sign of aqueduct obstruction.

name: Corpus callosum (context)
function: The great commissure linking the cerebral hemispheres, drawn as the sagittal-plate arch above the diencephalon; it forms the roof of the lateral ventricles and the superior boundary of the atlas scene.
contextNote: Context silhouette for the sagittal plate and 3D scene roof; not a diencephalic structure (hemisphere context).

afferent: Commissural fibers from cortical layers II/III of both hemispheres
efferent: Homotopic projections to the contralateral cortex

bloodSupply: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal branches) and posterior cerebral artery (splenial branches).

clinical.findings: Callosal injury or surgical section can impair transfer of information between hemispheres. In a typical left-language-dominant patient, an object presented only to the left visual field or explored by the left hand may not be named verbally despite recognition by the right hemisphere. Alien-hand phenomena are possible but not obligatory.
Callosal agenesis has variable clinical expression and may be associated with other malformations. It does not by itself establish hypothalamic dysfunction.

name: Internal capsule (context)
function: Compact deep white-matter structure between caudate/thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally. Its anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, retrolenticular and sublenticular parts carry different thalamocortical and descending projections, including motor, sensory, visual and auditory routes. It does not carry every corticofugal or thalamocortical connection.
contextNote: Context silhouette on plate-thalamus-mid and plate-coronal-thalamus; see also the subthalamus records for the pallidal (H1/H2) fasciculi looping through it.

afferent: Thalamocortical projections from sensory, motor and association thalamus
Descending cortical fibers from the corona radiata
efferent: Thalamic/cortical connections through anterior and posterior limbs
Descending corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine projections
Visual radiations in retrolenticular pathways and auditory radiations in sublenticular pathways

bloodSupply: Lenticulostriate branches of the MCA (genu/posterior limb), anterior choroidal artery (retrolenticular and inferior posterior limb), recurrent artery of Heubner (anterior limb).

clinical.findings: Small posterior-limb or genu infarcts can cause contralateral weakness or dysarthria without cortical signs. Sensory loss, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand depend on involved pathways; dysarthria-clumsy hand itself can be a lacunar capsular syndrome.

Retrolenticular optic-radiation injury can cause contralateral homonymous visual-field loss. Completeness and congruity depend on affected fibers and lesion extent; incongruity is not obligatory. Vascular supply is variable.

name: Lentiform nucleus (context silhouette)
function: Silhouette of the putamen and globus pallidus lateral to the internal capsule, shown on the transverse and coronal thalamic plates for orientation; the striatopallidal loops ending here gate movement through the ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamus.
contextNote: Context silhouette of the lentiform (putamen + globus pallidus) mass on plate-thalamus-mid and plate-coronal-thalamus. v19 (audit FAC-DI-008): the old sentence "basal-ganglia detail is out of scope for v1" was stale — v7/v8 shipped the detail it deferred, as the nucleus records nuc-putamen, nuc-globus-pallidus-internus, nuc-globus-pallidus-externus, nuc-caudate-head, nuc-caudate-body, nuc-caudate-tail, nuc-ventral-striatum and nuc-accumbens, and the capsule segments tract-internal-capsule-anterior-limb/-genu/-posterior-limb. This record is the silhouette that CONTAINS them; use the nucleus records for content.

afferent: Striatal input to the globus pallidus (direct and indirect pathway convergence)
efferent: Pallidal output via the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus (H2) to the motor thalamus

bloodSupply: Lenticulostriate branches of the MCA; anterior choroidal artery supplies the inferior and posterior pallidum.

clinical.findings: Putaminal or pallidal hemorrhage/infarction may cause motor or cognitive effects; dense hemiparesis often reflects adjacent internal-capsule injury rather than isolated lentiform injury.
Carbon monoxide and other toxic/metabolic exposures can affect basal-ganglia networks and produce movement disorders. Imaging and clinical patterns depend on the exposure and involved structures.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 16, basal-ganglia/internal-capsule anatomy, printed pp. 740-748 (PDF pp. 766-774).

name: Caudate nucleus (context silhouette)
function: C-shaped striatal silhouette along the lateral ventricle — head at the anterior limb of the internal capsule, body over the thalamus — drawn at the superior-anterior margin of the thalamic plates as striatal context.
contextNote: Context silhouette; see ctx-lenticular-nucleus and ctx-internal-capsule for adjacent context records.

afferent: Association/prefrontal corticostriatal input
Nigrostriatal dopamine and thalamostriatal inputs
efferent: Direct-pathway striatal output to GPi/SNr
Indirect-pathway output to GPe

bloodSupply: Medial lenticulostriate and anterior cerebral (recurrent artery of Heubner) perforators for the head; lateral lenticulostriate branches for the body.

clinical.findings: Head-of-caudate lacunes (Heubner territory) produce abulia, disinhibition and contralateral neglect, mimicking frontal-lobe lesions.

Huntington disease involves progressive striatal degeneration, including caudate and putamen, with motor, cognitive, and behavioral manifestations and additional brain involvement. Caudate atrophy may be evident on patient CT or MRI; the invariant atlas silhouette does not demonstrate disease-related volume loss.
